Key Characteristics & Etiology: Hypertrophy of circular muscle of pylorus peaking in male infants 3-6 weeks of age
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Progressive luminal narrowing of pyloric canal causing gastric outlet obstruction and severe emesis
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Non-bilious projectile vomiting after feeds olive-shaped RUQ mass; Red Flags: Severe dehydration hypokalemia
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Serum chemistry: hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis Abdominal US pyloric thickness >=4mm; Ramstedt pyloromyotomy

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Invagination of proximal bowel into distal lumen (ileocolic most common) in infants 3-12 months
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Bowel wall edema vascular compromise mucosal sloughing intestinal obstruction and potential perforation
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Paroxysmal colicky abdominal pain screaming with legs drawn up sausage-shaped RUQ mass red currant jelly stool
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Abdominal Ultrasound target/doughnut sign; Ultrasound-guided Air or Hydrostatic Contrast Enema reduction

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Anomalous intestinal rotation and fixation during embryogenesis resulting in narrow mesenteric root
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Twisting of bowel around superior mesenteric artery causing acute ischemia and total intestinal necrosis
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Sudden onset of bilious (green) vomiting in a neonate abdominal distension hematochezia shock; Red Flags: Peritonitis
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Upper GI contrast series showing corkscrew sign and Cecum in RUQ; Immediate emergency Ladd Procedure

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Congenital aganglionosis of distal bowel due to failure of neural crest cell migration
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Absence of parasympathetic ganglion cells in myenteric and submucosal plexuses preventing distal relaxation
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Failure to pass meconium <48h abdominal distension bilious vomiting blast sign on DRE; Red Flags: Enterocolitis (HAEC)
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Abdominal X-ray contrast enema transition zone; Gold Standard: Suction Rectal Biopsy showing no ganglion cells

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Persistent patent processus vaginalis allowing abdominal contents to herniate into inguinal canal
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Entrapment of bowel loop within hernia sac causing venous congestion ischemia and strangulation
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Painful tender non-reducible groin/scrotal swelling vomiting irritability; Red Flags: Strangulation peritonitis
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Clinical diagnosis pelvic ultrasound; Manual reduction under sedation if uncomplicated -> Elective surgical repair

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Accidental inhalation of foreign object (peanuts seeds small toys) into tracheobronchial tree in toddlers
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Mechanical airway obstruction causing air-trapping atelectasis or distal suppurative pulmonary infection
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Sudden choking paroxysmal cough unilateral monophonic expiratory wheeze diminished breath sounds; Red Flags: Asphyxia
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Expiratory CXR showing unilateral hyperinflation/atelectasis; Rigid Bronchoscopy under general anesthesia

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Accidental ingestion of disc/button batteries peaking in children <5 years of age
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Mucosal contact generates electrical current and hydroxide ions causing rapid liquefactive tissue necrosis
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Dysphagia drooling chest pain refusal to eat; Red Flags: Esophageal perforation tracheoesophageal fistula
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: AP/lateral X-ray showing double-ring/halo sign; Immediate Emergency Endoscopic Removal within 2 hours

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Accidental exposure or ingestion of organophosphate agricultural insecticides
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Inhibition of acetylcholinesterase enzyme causing acute acetylcholine accumulation and cholinergic crisis
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Salivation lacrimation urination defecation GI distress emesis (SLUDGE) miosis bradycardia muscle fasciculations
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Serum cholinesterase level blood atropinization test; High-dose Atropine Sulfate + Pralidoxime (2-PAM)

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Accidental or intentional acute ingestion of paracetamol >150 mg/kg in children
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Depletion of hepatic glutathione leads to accumulation of toxic reactive metabolite NAPQI causing hepatocyte necrosis
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Nausea vomiting right upper quadrant pain jaundice oliguria; Red Flags: Acute liver failure encephalopathy
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Serum paracetamol level plotted on Rumack-Matthew nomogram (>4h post-ingestion) LFTs INR; Intravenous N-acetylcysteine (NAC)

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Violent shaking or blunt impact in infants <1 year causing acceleration-deceleration forces
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Tearing of bridging meningeal veins and cerebral shear injury causing subdural hemorrhage and diffuse axonal damage
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Encephalopathy lethargy bulging fontanelle retinal hemorrhages seizures; Red Flags: Unexplained coma skeletal fractures
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Non-contrast CT head showing subdural hematomas skeletal survey fundoscopy; Mandatory Child Protection Reporting
